Action Plan:
- Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.
- Assess and optimize acute treatment for a likely migraine: evaluate current NSAID use and consider stronger analgesia. If ibuprofen dose is inadequate, adjust toward recommended dosing and/or switch to naproxen or add acetaminophen (paracetamol) with or without codeine; specific dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Prescribe appropriate acute medications today (naproxen or acetaminophen with/without codeine) with dosing details to be provided.
- Instruct patient to keep a headache diary over the coming days to identify triggers and response to treatment.
- Schedule follow-up in 1–2 weeks; instruct patient to contact sooner if symptoms worsen or develop red flags (e.g., vision changes, weakness, speech difficulty, fever, confusion).

Subjective:
- Chief complaint: Severe headache ongoing for about 3 days.
- Onset/duration/progression: Began ~3 days ago; gradually worsening; present most of the time with fluctuating intensity; worse by morning.
- Location/nature: Headache felt all over but mainly around the right eye; pain described as dull most of the time with intermittent sharpness.
- Severity: ~8/10.
- Associated symptoms: Photophobia (light hurts eyes), nausea/sick feeling, neck stiffness; no vomiting; no vision loss reported; difficulty focusing at work.
- Radiation: none noted.
- Aggravating/relieving: Ibuprofen tried for ~2 days without meaningful relief; using higher screen brightness/eye strain noted due to IT work.
- Past episodes: Has had headaches before; rarely had migraines; no prior migraine diagnosis; mother and sister have migraines.
- Medications: No regular medications; used ibuprofen (three tablets/day) prior to visit; no known drug allergies.
- Medical history: Headache history with family history of migraines; glasses wearer since age 5.
- Social history: IT worker; lives with three housemates; socially smokes and drinks.
- Review of systems: No fever, no rashes; no focal neurological symptoms reported (no weakness, no speech difficulty); some light sensitivity; no vomiting.

Objective:
- Symptoms documented by patient (not all objective exam findings are provided in transcript).
- Noted: neck stiffness reported by patient; photophobia with sensitivity to bright light; no reported vision loss; no vomiting; difficulty concentrating at work.
- Physical examination details and vitals are not documented in the transcript; no specific imaging or laboratory findings are provided.

Assessment & Plan:
1) Issue: Likely migraine headache (without aura), with possible genetic predisposition
   - Assessment: Migraine (without aura) is the leading consideration given unilateral-right eye–predominant pain, photophobia, nausea, gradual progression over 3 days, and family history of migraines.
   - Differential diagnoses (consistent with transcript and interview; as applicable):
     - Tension-type headache (medium likelihood) — dull, diffuse pain with stress/work factors; less consistent due to photophobia and nausea.
     - Meningitis/encephalitis (low) — neck stiffness and photophobia present; but no fever, AMS, or rapid progression.
     - Medication-overuse headache (low to medium) — prior NSAID use; pattern would typically require more prolonged use.
     - Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) (low) — young woman with persistent headache; no focal deficits or fever described; consider if symptoms persist or worsen.
2) Investigations planned:
   - No imaging or labs ordered today based on current history; reassess if red flags develop (e.g., fever, AMS, new focal deficits) or headache becomes more frequent/worsens.
3) Treatment planned:
   - Acute management: Offer stronger analgesia today (naproxen or acetaminophen with or without codeine); dosing specifics for naproxen/acetaminophen/codeine to be documented on prescription.
   - Optimize NSAID use: If continuing ibuprofen, ensure dosing adheres to recommended limits (up to two tablets, three times daily) or adjust therapy as above.
   - Headache diary: Initiate a diary to identify triggers and response to therapy.
   - Follow-up: Reassess in 1–2 weeks; sooner if headaches worsen or red flags arise.
   - Prophylaxis discussion: If headaches become more frequent, discuss preventive therapy at the next visit.
   - Return precautions: If vision changes worsen, new weakness, speech difficulties, or systemic symptoms develop, return promptly.
4) Referrals:
   - No referrals indicated at this time; reassess at follow-up if symptoms persist or worsen.
